He means something more than that. Cal doesn't know what yet. Dev walks out the gate toward Lowell with his hands in his pockets, past the cop in the tiara, and doesn't look back.

Margaux is waiting, one hand on the porch door, the light from inside making her a silhouette. His phone is warm in his hand. Somewhere down the hill, past the backyards of Elm Row, the lake is out there in the dark, and Priya is on the end of a dock.
Tick tock, Whitaker.

choices.label: Go up to the roof with Margaux

reaction.text: He texts Priya: u ok?? And then, because he's a coward, or because he's eighteen, or because Margaux is holding the door, he puts the phone in his pocket before he can see whether she answers.
He follows Margaux up three flights of a sorority house that smells like hairspray and old roses, past a framed portrait of a woman in pearls from 1958 who looks deeply disappointed in both of them.

choices.label: Go find Priya at the lake

reaction.text: Rain check. I have to... a friend's being a friend. Sorry.
Margaux's face doesn't move at all. That's how he knows it landed.
No you're not.

She goes inside. He's already running, down the side of the Kappa house, over a low stone wall, through somebody's backyard and a hedge, downhill in the dark toward the water, phone flashlight bouncing, calling her back and getting voicemail, voicemail, voicemail.

blocks.text: Act Three · After
EXT. KAPPA LAMBDA HOUSE, ROOF. NIGHT (11:05 P.M.)

Through a Kappa senior's bedroom, past a bed with eleven decorative pillows and a ring light, out a dormer window, onto slate. The roof pitches gently down to a flat stretch above the porch, rimmed with copper gutters gone green. Completely illegal. Completely gorgeous.

From up here you can see all of it. The party shrunk to a bowl of string lights. The black edge of the lake. And across campus, on the hill, the floodlit stone of WHITAKER COMMONS, his name lit up white against the dark like a sign over a motel.
Margaux produces a bottle of Ruinart from somewhere in the folds of her dress.
The house mom keeps it for when a sister gets engaged. Nobody's getting engaged this year. I checked.
She pops it with a dishcloth, quietly, like a professional. They pass the bottle back and forth. It's the first thing he's seen her actually drink all night.
She's different up here, a little. Shoes off, side by side on the slate, resoled heels to the wall. Knees up, arms around them, a posture he'd bet she has never once used in public.

They talk like two people raised by the same kind of money, because they were. Boarding school at twelve. Nannies who were fired for getting too attached. Parents who arrive for the photographs, stay through the cheese course, and leave before the speeches.
My nanny was Brazilian. Lúcia. She taught me to swear in Portuguese. My mother fired her when I said my first word and it was a Portuguese word for something you can't say at the club.
Mine was named Bridget. She taught me to play poker and gamble for Oreos. My father fired her when he found out I was beating her.
Your father fires people who lose?
My father fires people who make him feel things.

She laughs, really laughs, and then catches herself, and then asks, lightly, how Whitaker Lyle is doing this year, has the firm been busy, is it true they're buying up debt now instead of companies. It's one question too many. He sees her see that it was one too many.
She takes the bottle from him and says, without looking at him, “Don't bring up what I said on the lawn. About my family. I didn't say it.” He says, “Say what?” She almost smiles.
Then, out of nowhere, unguarded, looking across the dark at the Commons, the gothic arches lit from below:
Those buttresses are fake. They're not holding anything up. They bolted them on in 1994 to make it look old. I draw buildings, you know. When I can't sleep. I'd have done the whole thing in glass.
A beat. She hears herself. Her face closes like a compact.
I'm joking. Obviously. I can't draw a circle.
She hands him the bottle. Their fingers touch on the cold glass. Neither of them moves them right away. The whole night is tilted like the roof.

choices.label: Kiss her before either of you can think

reaction.text: He leans in. She meets him halfway, exactly halfway, not an inch more, like she measured.

She kisses him back like it's a decision she made in advance, maybe hours ago, maybe on the porch steps. It's controlled and very good and tastes like the champagne. Her hand goes flat against his chest. Then it fists in his shirt.
Then she pulls back, an inch, and studies him in the dark, frowning slightly, like she's surprised. Not by him. By something in herself she didn't put there and can't account for.
Huh.
Is that a review?
It's a note.

choices.label: “Why are you really up here with me?”

reaction.text: Why are you really up here with me?
Because you're interesting.
That's not the reason.
It's a reason.
It's a reason the way that dress is a dress.

Her eyes flick to his. She knows he means the tag. She doesn't know how he knows. For a second something very cold and very frightened goes across her face, and then she laughs it off and takes a long drink from the bottle.
They don't kiss. They sit six inches apart on a cold roof and don't kiss, and the not-kissing is louder than the party.

choices.label: Tell her something true: the notebooks

reaction.text: I write. Notebooks. Since I was a kid. Nobody's ever read them. Nobody even knows they exist. I don't know why I'm telling you that.

Margaux is quiet for a long time. Then she pulls her phone out and opens a photo album he can tell is hidden behind a passcode, and hands it to him. Pencil drawings, photographed in bad light. Buildings. Dozens. A library made of glass and timber. A boathouse that floats. A chapel with no walls at all, just a roof hovering on columns over a lake.
For real this time. Don't tell anyone. My father thinks architecture is a hobby for people who marry architects.
Two secret makers on a roof, holding each other's unread pages. It's the most dangerous moment of the night, because it's real, and both of them know it, and neither of them knows what to do with it.

blocks.text: EXT. KAPPA ROOF. NIGHT (11:40 P.M.)

The party has thinned below. Somebody's crying on the lawn, the good kind or the bad kind, impossible to tell from up here. The Ruinart is two-thirds gone. Margaux has his parka around her shoulders now, the St. Anselm's crest upside down on her back. She says it's ugly. She hasn't taken it off.
Between them on the slate, her phone lights up. The screen glows blue on both their faces.
MOM.

Margaux freezes. Not a flinch. A freeze. Every muscle goes still at once, like an animal in headlights, like a girl at a piano recital who has forgotten the next bar. It's the only unperformed fear he's seen on her all night, and it is total. Her hand doesn't move toward the phone. Her eyes don't move off it.
It rings out. Voicemail.
Three seconds of silence. Then it lights up again. MOM.

Cal reads all of it. Her hands, which have gone white at the knuckles around her knees. The way her shoulders have come up toward her ears. The way she's stopped breathing, actually stopped, the way people do underwater. He knows that posture. He's seen it in the mirror of a motel bathroom. He's seen it on himself, every time his father's name lights up a screen.
Whoever is calling, Margaux Vance is afraid of them. And whoever they are, they're going to keep calling.
The phone buzzes against the slate, inching toward the edge of the roof, toward the gutter, toward the three-story drop to the porch, as if it's trying to get away from her.
It's nothing. It's my mother. She does this. She's fine. I'm fine.

She isn't. Neither is he. Below them, the DJ plays the last song, and the string lights go off all at once, a hundred bulbs, and the lawn goes dark, and there's only the phone, lit, buzzing, and her face above it.

choices.label: Turn her phone face-down: “Let it ring.”

reaction.text: He reaches over and turns the phone face-down on the slate. The glow goes out. It keeps buzzing, muffled, like something trapped under a glass.
Let it ring.
She looks at him for a long time. Then she kisses him, hard, the first time, like she's trying to get somewhere fast.

She walks him back through the window to her own room two doors down: drawing tubes in the closet, a bed made with hospital corners. She locks the door. Checks it. Then she turns around and unzips her own dress, without ceremony, and steps out of it, and it lands inside out on the floor with the price tag face-up between them, white as a flag. They both look at it. She laughs, a real laugh, the first unpolished sound he's heard her make, and kicks the dress under the bed.

It's frank and a little competitive at first, both of them good at this and wanting the other to know it. She pushes him down onto the hospital corners and tells him what she wants in a low, precise voice, like directions to a driver. He does it better than she expected; her nails in his back say so. Then, somewhere in the middle, it changes. She says his name, just his first name, like a question, and opens her eyes, and he's looking at her, and it gets suddenly, terribly tender, slow, her forehead against his, and that scares them both more than anything else has all day.
After, she lies with her back to him and sets the rules to the wall.
Nobody knows. Not Priya, not your little friends across the hall. Nobody.
Okay.
At 1 a.m. he walks back to Lowell in her Kappa sweatshirt, because she's kept his parka. He can't stop smiling. He can't figure out why it feels like losing.

choices.label: “Who's scaring you?”

reaction.text: Who's scaring you?
She turns and looks at him like he just took her clothes off in front of the whole lawn. Then she smiles. It takes about a second to build, and it's flawless.
No one.
The lie of her life, delivered perfectly, with a little laugh at the end. If he hadn't been born into the same kind of house, he'd have believed it.
She stands, slips the parka off her shoulders and hands it back to him, folded. She leans down and kisses him on the cheek, very lightly, very correctly, like a hostess at the end of a dinner.
Goodnight, Whitaker.
She's furious at him for seeing it. She's also, he can tell, grateful, and she hates that more. He walks back to Lowell alone with the taste of the champagne going sour.

choices.label: Make a joke and climb back in the window, fast

reaction.text: Wow. Okay. Moms, right? Mine's in witness protection, it's a lot less phone. I should... it's late, I have a... radiator. Goodnight! Great roof!
He's back through the window before she can answer, because it was getting real, and he does what he always does when it gets real. He leaves his parka on her shoulders. He doesn't go back for it.
EXT. KAPPA ROOF. MOMENTS LATER
Margaux, alone on the slate, watches the window he went through. The phone lights up a third time. She picks it up.
He left.
A pause. A voice on the line, tinny and sharp.
No, Mom. I didn't.
She hangs up and pulls his ugly parka tighter around her and sits on the roof in the dark for a long time.

blocks.text: Act Three · After
EXT. TAMSIN LAKE, THE WHITLOCK BOATHOUSE DOCK. NIGHT (11:05 P.M.)

The boathouse at night is a cathedral for drowned things. The big doors on the water side stand open, and inside, in the dark, racing shells hang on their racks one above another, long and pale and ribbed, like the skeletons of something that used to swim.

The dock runs out from the boathouse thirty yards into the black. The lake is dead still. The moon is on it, a white road going nowhere. It's colder down here than on Elm Row, ten degrees colder, the water breathing it up.

Priya is at the very end of the dock in her underwear. Black bra, white cotton briefs, the slip dress in a puddle beside a bottle of mezcal with two inches left in it. She's barefoot. She's dancing. There's no music. She's spinning on the wet boards with her arms out like a kid playing helicopter, laughing at something nobody said.
CAL! You came! You came, you came. I knew you'd come, I said to Kevin, I said he'll come, he's got a rescuer face, it's tragic.

She talks faster than he's ever heard her, which is saying something. Her pupils are huge in the moonlight, black lakes. He can see the orange bottle sticking out of the pocket of the dress on the boards, cap off.

Did you know Ophelia didn't fall? Everybody says she fell. She didn't fall. She went in singing. She went in singing, Cal, that's not falling, that's a choice, that's an exit, that's the best exit in Shakespeare and nobody gives her credit because she's a girl and she's sad.
Priya. Hey. Can we come back from the edge a little?
Swim with me. The lake's like eight hundred feet deep. Someone died in it. A boy. The rowers say he's still down there. They say if you swim at night he grabs your ankle to say hi. I want to say hi.

Through the open boathouse doors, high in the rafters above the hanging shells, his phone flashlight catches something. An old wooden oar, mounted crosswise on the beams, painted black. Lettered in white, by hand, faded almost to nothing: T.C. SWIM ON.
He looks at it a second too long. When he looks back at the end of the dock, she's on the edge, toes curled over, arms up.
Watch me go in singing.
She dives. A clean dive, a good one, a theater kid's dive, all line. The black water closes over her with almost no splash, and the rings spread out, and spread, and flatten.
He waits for her to come up laughing. Two seconds. Four. Six. The water's flat again. The moon is back on it like nothing happened. She isn't coming up.

choices.label: Jump in after her

reaction.text: He's in before he thinks. His body remembers the way it remembers stairs: shoes kicked, three steps, a racing dive off the end of the dock, flat and long. Two and a half years of St. Anselm's swim. It all comes back like a reflex he didn't know he still had.

Cold that stops your heart. Actually stops it, for a beat, a full-body clench. Then black. Total black. Not dark, black, like being inside closed eyes. No sound but his own blood, huge and slow in his ears, the underwater roar.

He sweeps with his arms. Nothing. Nothing. He goes deeper, lungs starting to burn, the cold pushing in at his temples. Nothing. Then his fingers close on something soft and moving. An arm. Her arm. He finds her arm.

choices.label: Stay on the dock, phone flashlight, shout her name

reaction.text: He drops to his knees on the end of the dock and shines his phone flashlight down into the water. It goes in about a foot and stops, like hitting a wall. Black.
PRIYA! PRIYA!
Eleven seconds. He counts them later. Eleven seconds that last about a year, the flashlight on black water, his own voice coming back off the boathouse wall.

Then she surfaces, twenty feet out, gasping, laughing, triumphant. Then not laughing. Her face changes. She goes under, comes back up, grabbing at her leg. A cramp. The cold. She's not a strong swimmer, it turns out. Ophelia never was.
He goes in anyway. Shoes and all. He was always going to.

choices.label: Grab your phone and call Dev

reaction.text: His hands are shaking so hard he almost drops the phone. He hits DEV (ACROSS THE HALL, HAS DRILL). It doesn't even finish the first ring.
What's wrong?
Priya. The lake. The boathouse. She went in and she's not, she's not coming...
And while he's still talking, she surfaces fifteen feet out, coughing, choking, flailing for the dock, too far.
I'm coming. Get her out. Get her out, Cal, I'm coming.

Cal drops the phone on the boards, still connected, and goes in. Dev is running down the hill from Lowell in the dark. He'll arrive in seven minutes, in flip-flops, carrying every towel from the third-floor bathroom.

blocks.text: EXT. BOATHOUSE DOCK. NIGHT (11:30 P.M.)

He gets her to the ladder. He gets her up the ladder, pushing from below, her bare heel catching him in the jaw. They collapse on the dock, both soaked, both heaving, lake water streaming out of their hair and noses. He's in jeans that weigh forty pounds. She's shaking so hard her teeth sound like dice.

Dev comes thundering down the dock in flip-flops and a Rockets T-shirt with his arms full of towels, and drops to his knees, and wraps Priya up like a burrito without asking anybody's permission. He puts two fingers on her wrist and counts, lips moving, like he's done it before. He doesn't say anything to Cal. He just throws him a towel without looking.

Priya is curled on her side on the wet boards. And all at once the mania drains out of her, the way water drains out of a bathtub, with a sound. The speed is gone. The bit is gone. What's left is a girl in her underwear on a dock, crying, ugly, big gasping sobs, the realest she's been all day.
I'm not okay. I'm not okay. I'm just loud.
He doesn't know what to do with his hands. He puts one on her back. She grabs his wrist and holds on with both hands, hard enough to bruise.
She says something through her teeth into the boards, crying. He has to lean down to hear it. “Your mom's an idiot. Your mom's an idiot. Who leaves? Who leaves you?” He doesn't answer. He can't.
Promise me. Promise me you won't tell anybody. Not the RA, not health services, not my mom, God, not my mom. Nobody. Swear to me.
Priya...
Swear, Cal.
I swear.
He means it. He'll regret it. Both of those are already true.

Then light. A big white flashlight beam swinging down the hill from the path, from the direction of the athletic fields, bouncing, getting closer. A radio crackling. A voice, bored and official, calling out.

blocks.name: SECURITY OFFICER
blocks.text: Hey! Boathouse is closed after dark! Who's down there?

Campus security. Coming down to the boathouse. Thirty seconds away, maybe less. Priya's pupils are still enormous. The orange bottle with someone else's name on it is sitting in the pocket of her dress on the dock in plain sight, next to an almost empty bottle of mezcal. She's in no shape to be caught. She knows it. She looks at Cal with her whole face.

choices.label: Run, both of you, laughing and soaking

reaction.text: He grabs the dress and the bottle and her hand, and they run. Barefoot across the athletic fields in the dark, soaking, the wet grass freezing, the flashlight sweeping behind them and missing. She starts laughing halfway across the soccer pitch, and then he's laughing, and they can't stop. It's joyful and stupid and she's alive.
Dev runs beside them in his flip-flops, losing one, then the other, swearing in Igbo the whole way, carrying the towels like a man rescuing a flag.
They make it to Lowell. Up three flights, dripping, slipping, shushing each other too loudly. As they fall through the door onto the third floor, Gerald bangs once, enormously, like a gong.
Gerald approves. Gerald says we're the best thing that's ever happened to this building.

choices.label: Use the name: “I'm Cal Whitaker. We're fine, officer.”

reaction.text: He stands up, dripping, into the flashlight beam, and does the voice. His father's voice. Calm and warm and faintly amused.
Evening. Cal Whitaker. We're fine, officer. Just a dumb freshman swim. My fault. We're heading back to Lowell now.
The beam drops. The officer, a big guy in his fifties, looks up the hill at the lit name on the Commons, then back at Cal.

reaction.name: SECURITY OFFICER
reaction.text: Whitaker. Oh. Sorry, son. Sorry to bother you. You kids get warm, okay? You need a cart?
It works instantly. That's the worst part. The man apologizes to him.
Dev, holding the towels, looks at the ground the whole time.
On the walk back up the hill, Priya, wrapped in a towel, quiet now, says: “That was gross.” Then, a minute later: “Thank you.”

choices.label: Take the blame, let Priya slip away

reaction.text: He shoves the dress and the bottles into her arms and points, without a word, to the dark mouth of the boathouse. She goes. He walks up the dock into the flashlight alone, hands up, dripping.
Just me. I went swimming. It was stupid. I'm sorry.

The officer writes him up: trespassing in a closed athletic facility, alcohol on the premises, a dorm-conduct report that'll go to his RA and the Dean of Students' office. He asks for Cal's name. Cal gives him the real one. He watches the man's pen pause on the W.
Dev steps up beside him, towels and all. “Me too. I was swimming too.” He wasn't. He gets written up anyway. He doesn't even look at Cal when he does it. Cal will think about that for a long time.
Behind them, in the dark of the boathouse, Priya crouches between the racked shells, wrapped in a towel, and watches him do it. She doesn't make a sound. She'll never forget it.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD FLOOR HALLWAY / CAL'S SINGLE. NIGHT (1:14 A.M.)

Cal comes up the stairs of Lowell two at a time and then one at a time and then stops on the landing, in Margaux Vance's Kappa Lambda sweatshirt, which smells like her perfume and like her skin under it, the sleeves too short on him, KAPPA LAMBDA across his chest in white like a confession. Nobody knows. He promised. He's grinning in the dark like an idiot and he can't make it stop, and underneath the grin there's something cold he doesn't want to look at.

Cal comes up the stairs of Lowell alone with his parka over his arm and the champagne gone sour in his mouth. He keeps seeing her face over the lit phone. He keeps seeing the smile she built in a second, flawless, to cover it. He knows how long it takes to build a smile like that. Years.

Cal comes up the stairs of Lowell alone, without his parka, cold in a T-shirt. He left it on her shoulders. He left. He's very good at leaving. He tells himself it was a good joke. It was a fine joke. He keeps telling himself, and it keeps not working.

Cal is sitting on the floor of the third-floor hallway with his back against his own door, still in wet jeans, dripping slowly onto a carpet that has survived two centuries and will survive this. Lake water in his shoes. Lake in his ears. Priya is across the hall now, asleep on Dev's floor under every towel the third floor owns. He gave her his last dry shirt. He can't stop shivering. He can't stop hearing his own voice shouting her name off the boathouse wall.
In his back pocket, a carbon copy of a campus-security conduct report has gone to pulp. He can still read his own name on it. Everyone always can.
His phone buzzes against the floorboards. He almost doesn't look. Then he does.

Not Denise. Not a group chat. The contact he has saved as DAD, which has not sent him a text written by its own owner since his eighteenth birthday in March, when it said: Happy birthday. Call Denise re: the trust.

msgs.text: Denise says you were rude. Fine.
I saw the video. One of the brothers sent it before you'd climbed down off the table.
It was funny. Next time make it funny at someone else's expense.
Heard you made an impression on Elm Row tonight. Good.
Brooks Hadley will reach out about rush. The Rho matters, Cal. It's how this place works.
The Herald will want a legacy quote. Don't give them one.

blocks.text: Cal laughs out loud, alone, a short ugly bark. Too late. He gave them a very good one. He's a little proud of it. He's a little sick about it.
He thinks of a red recorder light, and a girl's face going still, and what he said into it. Too late for that too.

Then the dots. His father is typing. His father, at 1:14 in the morning, on a Monday, in New York or wherever he is, is typing a text to his son with his own thumbs. The dots go on for a long time. Cal watches them the way you watch a wave before it breaks.

Then they stop. Nothing comes. Just: Read 1:14 AM, under Cal's side of the thread, because his father can see that he's seen it. Both of them looking at the same empty screen from two hundred miles apart, both of them waiting for the other one to blink.
Down the hall, Gerald bangs once, low, like a judge.
This is the first thing his father has asked of him in person, so to speak, in a year. Not a favor. A promise. And he's asking for it the way he asks for everything: as if it's already been given.

choices.label: Give him what he wants: “I'll rush.”
choices.remember: Your father will hold you to that.

msgs.text: I'll rush.
Good.

reaction.text: A minute goes by. Cal is about to put the phone down. Then:

msgs.text: Proud of you.

reaction.text: Three words. Well, two and a half. The words he has waited about eight years to hear, since the last time his father said them, at a swim meet when Cal was ten and still thought winning was the same thing as being wanted. He reads them nine times. They're for the wrong reason. They're for the Rho, for the wall, for the jaw and the name. He knows that.
He hates how good it feels. He hates it so much he has to put the phone face-down on the floor and press the heels of his hands into his eyes until he sees colors.

choices.label: “You didn't come. You don't get to ask me for anything.”

msgs.text: You didn't come. You don't get to ask me for anything.

reaction.text: Typed and sent before he can stop his thumbs. Delivered. Read. Read 1:16 AM.
Then a long silence. Long enough that he thinks that's it, that's the end, his father will simply let it sit there like an unsigned contract until it expires.

Then the phone lights up in his hand and starts to ring. Not a text. A call. DAD. His father calling, with his voice, at 1:17 in the morning. It hasn't happened in so long that for a second Cal doesn't recognize the screen.
He watches it ring. Five times. Six. He declines it. His thumb is shaking.
Thirty seconds later: a voicemail. Forty-one seconds long. He looks at the little red dot for a long time. He doesn't listen to it. Not yet.

choices.label: Leave him on read.

reaction.text: He doesn't answer. He just lets it sit. Under his father's message, in small gray letters: Read 1:15 AM. He knows his father can see it. That's the point. That's the only weapon he's ever had.
Five minutes later:

msgs.text: I can see you read it.

reaction.text: Nothing. He reads that too. Then, at 1:31, eleven more minutes of dots and no dots and dots:

msgs.text: Your mother would have come. That's the joke.

reaction.text: Cal stares at it for a long, long time. Gerald doesn't bang. The building holds its breath.

His father has not said the word mother, not out loud, not in writing, not once, in seven years. Not when Cal asked, at twelve, and at thirteen, and then stopped asking. And now here it is, at 1:31 in the morning, as a punchline. He doesn't know whether it's an insult, or an apology, or a man who's had four Scotches telling the truth by accident. He doesn't know which would be worse.

blocks.text: INT. LOWELL HOUSE, THIRD FLOOR HALLWAY. NIGHT (1:35 A.M.)

Across the hall, Dev's door opens. Dev stands there in a Houston Rockets T-shirt and plaid pajama pants, wide awake, holding a mug of chamomile like a man holding a candle in a power outage. The bunk bed behind him is very, very level.

Across the hall, Dev eases out of his room and pulls the door almost shut behind him. Through the gap: Priya, asleep on his floor in a nest of towels and his Astros hoodie, one arm flung over her eyes. A plate beside her with crusts on it. Dev made her eat toast. Two slices, with butter, sitting on the floor with her until she finished. It's a quietly enormous thing, and he'll never mention it.
I don't sleep great. Long year.

He doesn't ask if Cal's okay. He doesn't ask anything. He just slides down the wall onto the hallway carpet across from Cal, his back against his own door, mug on his knee, and sits. Cal sits down across from him. Two boys on a hallway floor at 1:35 a.m., six feet of two-hundred-year-old carpet between them, each of them holding something.
Gerald bangs. Loud. The pipes shiver all the way down the hall.
Your radiator's been doing that all night.
That's Gerald. Priya named him.
Of course she did.
He raises the mug toward Cal's room.
Gerald says hi.
Dev turns his mug a quarter turn on his knee, and almost smiles. “Poker chips, man,” he says, to nobody, and that's all he says about it.
Dev looks at the ceiling. “Chidi would've stayed up too. He'd have made me do the impressions.” He says the name like he's testing whether the floor will hold.
Your dad never did come up from parking, huh.
It's not an accusation. It's a door left open. Dev saw the car pull away at 2:15 this afternoon, and has known all day, and has carried it for him like the box marked BOOKS.

Dev blows on the tea. Waits. He's good at waiting. Cal is starting to understand that Dev is good at a lot of things that don't look like anything: waiting, noticing, carrying. He's looking at Cal's face the way a doctor looks at an X-ray, not with alarm, just with attention, which is rarer.
Cal can feel it coming. The question Dev isn't going to ask. Are you okay. It's sitting right there in the hallway between them like a third person.

choices.label: Tell Dev the truth about tonight and his father

reaction.text: He tells him. Not all of it. More than he's told anyone. The car service. Denise. The draft he never sent at 6:02 a.m. The text at 1:14.
The promise he made. The two words he got for it.
The fight. The call he declined. The voicemail he hasn't played.
The read receipt. The word mother, used as a punchline.
Dev listens like a doctor. He doesn't interrupt. He doesn't fix it. When Cal runs out, he's quiet for a while. Then:
For what it's worth? I'd have driven you.
It's nothing. It's a sentence. It's everything. Cal has to look at the ceiling for a while.

choices.label: “All good, man. Great night.”

reaction.text: All good, man. Great night. Truly. Top-five night. Just, you know. Wired.
The smooth lie. The one he does best. Dev nods slowly, the nod of someone who respects the lies people need, because he's needed a few.
Okay. I'm across the hall.

He gets up, knees cracking, and goes back in. He leaves his door cracked open, a two-inch stripe of lamplight across the hall carpet, all night long. Cal notices at 3 a.m. when he gets up to pee. It's still open at 5.

choices.label: “Why are you awake, Dev?”

reaction.text: Why are you awake, Dev?
Dev looks at him. Then at his tea. He turns the mug a full circle on his knee before he answers.
I'm nine months into a really long year.

He doesn't explain. Cal doesn't push. He wants to, every reflex he has says find the soft place and press, but he doesn't. Gerald bangs, and neither of them makes a joke about it. They just sit there. Two boys on a hallway floor in the middle of the night, each of them holding something heavy, neither of them putting it down, both of them a little less alone with it.

blocks.text: INT. CAL'S SINGLE. NIGHT (2:02 A.M.)

Cal at the bay window. The Quad empty and silver below. At the bottom of the hill, Tamsin Lake lies flat and bright under the moon, holding whatever it holds. Across the grass, the floodlit name on the Commons, still on, never off, WHITAKER, eighteen inches tall, burning all night for nobody.

He takes a new notebook out of the box. Black Moleskine, still in its plastic. He tears the plastic off. Clicks the pen four times. Writes the date at the top of the first page: August 24. Then crosses it out, because it isn't anymore, and writes August 25.
His phone lights up on the sill. A push alert. THE WHITLOCK HERALD: MOVE-IN: WHO GETS IN? By Nora Castellanos.

He reads it standing up. It's really good: angry, funny, precise, the thirty-eight percent, the drunk Kappa on affirmative action for people who deserve it. Two-thirds of the way down, he finds himself.

“At Kappa Lambda's Sunset on the Lawn, as two hundred students chanted the name of the student center, one third-generation legacy climbed onto a keg table and raised a glass: ‘To my father, who couldn't be here, which is the most Whitaker sentence ever spoken.’ The crowd loved it. It was, at least, honest about whose name was on the building.” Word for word. She got every word. He laughs, once, and then he doesn't.

“‘You get a name you didn't earn, and everyone acts like it's a gift,’ said Cal Whitaker, a third-generation legacy whose grandfather's name is carved over the student center. ‘It's not a gift. It's a loan. And you spend your whole life finding out what the interest rate is.’ It was the best sentence anyone said to this reporter all day. It's worth asking why the person who said it got in without having to.” In full. Beautifully. Damningly. He's proud of the sentence. She's used it like a scalpel. Both true.

“Asked how he got in, one legacy freshman instead asked this reporter whether her own admissions essay was ‘about your abuela.’ The quote is printed here in full, because it answers the question better than anything else he said.” His own words, in her font, forever. He reads it four more times. It doesn't get shorter.

“One freshman, who identified himself to the Herald as Cal Pruitt, which is not his name, declined to discuss his admission and offered to buy this reporter coffee instead. Pruitt Hall was built in 1868 and has never once lied about who it is.” He laughs so hard he has to put the phone down. He's a running joke on day one. He sort of loves it.
“One legacy, asked how he got in, offered to buy this reporter coffee in lieu of an answer. This reporter has a meal plan.” He laughs out loud, alone. She's funny. He hates that. He doesn't.

He scrolls. He scrolls again, slower. He isn't in it. Not his name, not his face, not one sentence. She kept her word. He didn't know until right now how much he expected her not to, and he stands at the window with the phone and that small, strange fact for a long time.
He picks up the pen. He writes one line in the new notebook. We don't see it. He looks at it for a while. He doesn't cross it out.
INT. THE WHITLOCK HERALD, BASEMENT OF PRUITT HALL. SAME TIME

A basement newsroom, pipes along the ceiling, old front pages framed on cinder block. Empty except for one desk lamp and Nora, alone. On her screen, the piece is live. She's just hit PUBLISH. She sits back. She doesn't celebrate. She takes a breath like she's been holding it since June.
Then she reaches under the desk and pulls out a shoebox. A worn one, a Payless box, the corners held with packing tape gone amber. She lifts the lid.

Inside: airmail letters, the blue tissue-paper kind, dozens, written in Spanish in a young man's slanting hand. And on top, a Polaroid. A grinning young man in a Rho sweatshirt, standing on a wooden dock with a lake behind him, squinting into the sun, one hand up like he's about to wave at whoever's holding the camera.
She turns it over. On the back, in an old woman's careful, shaky ballpoint: Tomás, Tamsin Lake, oct. 1991.

Nora gets up. Above her desk there's a corkboard, mostly empty. Pinned to it already: a printout of the Sigma Kappa Rho composite, 1991-1992. Thirty-four faces in ovals. And one oval in the pledge row with nothing in it but felt.
She pins the Polaroid beside it, carefully, with a red pushpin, smoothing the corner flat with her thumb.
Hi, tío.
She takes an index card from her desk and writes on it, in block capitals, pressing hard enough to dent the card: WHO WAS ON THE DOCK? She pins it under the photograph.
She looks at it a long time. Then she reaches over and kills the lamp.
CUT TO BLACK.
